brut.title: Recent storms kept Phoenix workers busy

webpage.text:
Recent storms kept Phoenix workers busy

* Phoenix officials expect to have to pay thousands for repairs
 * The Police%2C Fire%2C streets%2C parks and Public Works departments have all been "very%2C very busy"
 * A tactical operations center%2C which brings together multiple city departments%2C was activated during the storm

Powerful floods Aug. 19 charged through Phoenix homes, overflowed washes, spilled into canals and clogged Phoenix streets with mud and debris.

City workers spent the days following the monsoon storm — the second major storm this month — inspecting or clearing the damage.

Although city officials didn't have a cost estimate for the cleanup efforts, Phoenix will no doubt have to pay thousands of dollars for repairs.

The Police, Fire, streets, parks and Public Works departments have all been "very, very busy," city spokeswoman Toni Maccarone said.

Workers even had to used heavy equipment to remove debris and silt on south, north and northeast Phoenix streets.

The good news: Phoenix officials on Tuesday had prepared when they saw that two storms would converge — one that would hit south Phoenix and the other that would strike the northern part of the city. They activated a tactical operations center, which can bring together multiple city departments.

"I'm extremely proud of the ingenuity and efficiency by the city departments in meeting the overwhelming demand," said Kevin Kalkbrenner, Phoenix's Homeland Security and Emergency Management director.

Fire Department

Kalkbrenner said the departments received 51 calls for rescues Tuesday, five of which were in Phoenix.

But because Phoenix has a mutual-aid response system whereby Valley fire departments respond to emergencies regardless of municipal boundaries, Phoenix firefighters responded to a portion of those.

Fire Capt. Mark Vanacore said the storm was so powerful, about 200 firefighters from across the Valley were on duty Tuesday.

Firefighters worked seven rescues involving cars and flooded homes and washes at the height of the storm from 6 to 10 a.m., he said.

"Everybody that called for help was in need of our assistance," Vanacore said. "We had the resources. Even though we had an unprecedented number of rescues we were able to get to everybody that needed help in an extremely timely fashion."

No one was injured, he said.

Fire officials say there are no extra costs for the department when it conducts rescues because the firefighters are "all on duty, standing ready to rescue, treat, transport" 24 hours a day, seven days a week, spokeswoman Shelly Jamison said.

Parks and Recreation

Officials had to close the gates to several washes at the Cave Creek Wash Recreation Area after Tuesday's storms, and residents could not use the trails that cross the washes.

But the real damage came a week earlier when rain caused a rock slide in South Mountain Park. The Parks and Recreation Department closed Summit and San Juan roads so the crews could removed debris and boulders from the roads.

The slide happened halfway up Summit Roadat about the 2-mile mark in the park.

City officials kept the roads closed so engineers could inspect the damage more closely.

There was "a large volume of rain. It triggered this major slide," parks spokesman David Urbinatosaid.

Water Services

Tuesday's stormshammered north Phoenix, and water spilled over the banks of Skunk Creek Wash, flooding a Central Arizona Project Canal with brown, murky water, said Kathryn Sorensen, Water Services director.

That didn't bode wellfor the Union Hills Water Treatment Plant downstream of the canal.

However, the city was able to close the intakes before the plant could be contaminated, Sorensen said.

"We saw it coming and we have meters on the canal, which are water-quality sensors, and they gave us notice of what was coming our way," she said. "We were able to close the intake into the Union Hills plant so the muddy water passed us."

The plant is one of five that supply Phoenix with clean drinking water.

The city was able to "continue reliable, high-quality water deliveries during this storm event," Sorensen said Tuesday.

The intakes have since been reopened, and officials are monitoring the water quality, but found no problems as of Wednesday, spokeswoman Victoria Welch said.

None of the other water-treatment plants in Phoenix were affected by the flooding.

Neighborhood flooding

Homeowners in south Phoenix met with city officials Monday night to discuss flood damage from the Aug. 12storm.

Residents near 27th Avenue and Dobbins Road said it will cost them thousands of dollars to repair or replace homes affected by the storm.

Few people said they had flood insurance because the area is not in a designated flood area.

City officials said the city will conduct evaluations for the flood-damage area in the future.

Homeowners left the meeting unhappy and one remarked, "What we got tonight is a lot of political rhetoric that leads to nowhere."

Republic reporter Ryan Van Velzer contributed to this article.

webpage.text:
'Life-threatening' floods possible in Southwest this weekend

Heavy rains and life-threatening flash flooding from the remnants of Hurricane Norbert and Tropical Storm Dolly are possible in the Southwest this weekend, the National Hurricane Center warns.

"Excessive rain is likely in some areas with the chance of life-threatening flash flooding," said AccuWeather meteorologist Ken Clark, who adds the floods will be due to the region's rocky terrain, steep hillsides and arroyos. Runoff is often very rapid and can fill the typically dry stream beds.

The bulk of the rain will be centered on Arizona and western New Mexico, reports AccuWeather meteorologist Alex Sosnowski.

In Arizona, "showers and thunderstorms will increase in coverage Saturday and Sunday, with periods for heavy rain both days, and continuing through Monday at many different locations across the region," according to an online forecast from the National Weather Service in Phoenix.

Arizona has seen a wetter-than-normal monsoon season this year; a thunderstorm brought rain, gusty winds and blowing dust to Phoenix and some surrounding areas Thursday night.

Some rain will also reach southern Nevada, southern Utah, southwestern Colorado and part of Southern California, Sosnowski said. Some scattered thunderstorms and locally heavy rainfall could dampen parts of the L.A. Basin and San Diego metro area early next week, according to the Weather Channel.

Eastern Pacific hurricanes seldom affect the U.S., but occasionally a storm's remnants can bring heavy rain to California, the Southwest and sometimes to places as far east as Oklahoma.

Hurricane Norbert is now near the western coast of the Baja Peninsula in Mexico, where hurricane warnings have been issued, the Weather Channel reports. In addition, tropical storm warnings have been extended farther north along the peninsula.

As of 11 a.m. ET, the center of Norbert was located about 140 miles west of Cabo San Lucas, Mexico, and had maximum sustained winds of 90 mph, making it a Category 1 hurricane, the hurricane center reported.

It was tracking to the northwest at 8 mph. A slow weakening is expected during the next 48 hours, the hurricane center predicts.

Contributing: Associated Press
